Gumbo has three distinct meanings in English. The first is by far the most well-known, but knowing all three will give you a complete picture of the word.
Meaning 1 — A thick, hearty stew (the main and most common meaning)

Gumbo is a famous dish from Louisiana, a state in the southern United States. Think of it as a rich, thick, deeply flavored stew — somewhere between a soup and a stew in consistency — that is always served over white rice.

What makes gumbo special and different from a regular stew:

It always starts with a roux. A roux is a mixture of fat (oil or butter) and flour that is cooked slowly over heat. Depending on how long you cook it, it turns from pale white to golden to deep chocolate-brown. This cooked roux is the backbone of gumbo — it gives the dish its thickness, its deep color, and much of its flavor.

It is built on the "holy trinity." This is what Louisiana cooks call the base of three vegetables used in almost every gumbo: onion, celery, and bell pepper. These are cooked together first and form the flavor foundation of the dish.

It contains protein. A gumbo almost always includes some combination of meat or seafood. Common choices include chicken, andouille sausage (a smoky, spiced pork sausage), shrimp, crab, or oysters. Many gumbos mix proteins — for example, chicken and sausage gumbo, or seafood gumbo.

It is thickened by one (or both) of two special ingredients:

  • Okra — a green vegetable that releases a natural slippery substance when cooked, which thickens the stew
  • Filé powder — a fine powder made from dried, ground sassafras leaves, which is stirred in near the end of cooking and also thickens and flavors the dish

It is a one-pot dish. Everything cooks together in a single large pot, and the long, slow cooking melds all the flavors into something greater than the sum of its parts. A good gumbo often simmers for hours.

It reflects a mixing of cultures. Louisiana's history involved French, Spanish, African, Native American, and Caribbean influences, and gumbo is a direct expression of that cultural blending. Different families and communities have their own versions, and debates about the "correct" way to make gumbo are taken quite seriously in Louisiana.

When served, a ladleful of gumbo is spooned over a mound of steamed white rice placed in the center of a bowl. The rice absorbs the thick, flavorful liquid.
Meaning 2 — The okra plant or its pods

In certain regional dialects, especially in parts of the American South, the Caribbean, and West Africa, gumbo is simply another word for okra — the green, pod-shaped vegetable mentioned above. If someone in these regions says "I'm going to the market to buy some gumbo," they mean okra, not the stew. This usage is less common in everyday modern English but still appears and is worth knowing.
Meaning 3 — A type of heavy, sticky clay soil

Gumbo also refers to a specific kind of soil found in parts of the American Midwest and Great Plains — particularly in states like Oklahoma, Kansas, and Texas. This soil is made up of very fine clay particles. When it is dry, it can be hard and cracked. But when it gets wet from rain, it becomes extremely thick, sticky, heavy, and slippery — almost like wet cement or thick mud that clings to everything it touches.

Farmers and builders find gumbo soil particularly difficult to work with because wet gumbo can clog machinery, make roads impassable, and stick to boots like glue. People in these regions often say something like "the roads turned to gumbo after the rain" — meaning the ground became a sticky, muddy mess.
Meaning 4 — A rich mixture of things (figurative use)

Because the dish called gumbo is famous for blending many different ingredients and cultural traditions together into one pot, the word gumbo is sometimes used figuratively (not literally) to describe any rich, complex mixture of different elements — especially cultures, ideas, sounds, or influences.

For example:

  • "New Orleans is a gumbo of French, African, and Caribbean cultures."
  • "His music is a gumbo of jazz, blues, and funk."

In this figurative sense, calling something a "gumbo" suggests it is diverse, layered, deeply flavored by multiple influences, and that all the parts have blended together into something unified and rich.
Quick summary of all four meanings

• Meaning 1 (most common): A thick Louisiana stew made with a roux, the "holy trinity" of vegetables, meat or seafood, and okra or filé powder — served over rice
  • Meaning 2 (regional): Another word for the okra vegetable
  • Meaning 3: A type of very sticky, heavy clay soil that becomes muddy and difficult when wet
  • Meaning 4 (figurative): A rich, complex mixture or blend of different things, cultures, or influences
